extracted.intended_audience: journalism scholars, newsroom professionals, platform operators, and students of media/communication
extracted.subtask_short: newsroom editorial decisions under social algorithms
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating and making editorial and gatekeeping choices in newsrooms taking into account (and negotiating with) social media distribution algorithms and related metrics. Focus is on how journalists' informal beliefs ('folk theories') about algorithms shape selection, framing, resource allocation, and routines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Traditional newsworthiness / news values
rubrics_metrics.description: Standards for determining what becomes news, including timeliness, geographic location and proximity to audience, sensationalism, extreme valence, novelty, celebrity, and controversy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These long-standing news values remain foundational in gatekeeping; algorithmic considerations are negotiated against them and do not necessarily supplant them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engagement as primary algorithmic metric
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists overwhelmingly perceive engagement (liking, sharing, commenting, watch time, etc.) as the main factor that causes social media algorithms to surface content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is no consensus on how engagement is measured; engagement may be operationalized differently over time or across platforms. Journalists treat engagement both as user-interest signal and as platforms' means to increase ad revenue/retention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publisher attributes (size, brand, payment, relationships, ideology)
rubrics_metrics.description: Attributes of the news organization—its size/brand, relationships with platforms, willingness to pay/promote content, and perceived political ideology—are believed to influence algorithmic visibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Large/established outlets may receive preferential treatment or have better platform ties; smaller outlets may be forced to 'pay to play.' Perceived ideological alignment can lead to claims (or perceptions) of promotion/suppression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content medium/format preferences
rubrics_metrics.description: Different media formats are perceived to perform differently in algorithms; e.g., Facebook 'prefers video and prefers images…the hierarchy from most engaging to least engaging is videos, images, text, links.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Format choice (video vs image vs text vs links) is an actionable factor for distribution strategy; newsrooms may prioritize richer media to satisfy platform signals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Platform-specific algorithmic differences
rubrics_metrics.description: Algorithms differ by platform: Facebook seen as heavy-handed and opaque; Twitter as a lighter-touch, follower/retweet-driven system; Reddit as more community/user-moderated and rule-driven.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tailor posting and engagement strategies by platform. Treat Facebook as requiring pre-post optimizations; treat Reddit as community-oriented; treat Twitter as relying on network amplification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Posting frequency and timing constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific posting practices are believed to influence distribution (example: avoid posting the same story on Facebook within 48 hours because the algorithm may demote or 'penalize' repeated posts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enforce platform-specific timing rules to avoid reduced visibility; spacing of posts considered part of routine editorial practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shareability / trending as a metric of newsworthiness
rubrics_metrics.description: Shareability (the likelihood a story will be shared/commented on) and whether a topic is trending on social media are treated as new inputs into assessments of newsworthiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors may prioritize or reframe stories to increase shareability; trending signals can shift perceived importance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantifiable engagement vs engaged journalism tension
rubrics_metrics.description: Algorithms define engagement through narrow, quantifiable metrics (clicks, shares) which may conflict with engaged journalism's broader goals of deep community engagement and public interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists must weigh short-term quantifiable metrics against long-term civic or community value; avoid equating clicks with public importance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resource allocation based on algorithmic performance
rubrics_metrics.description: Editorial resources (reporter time, social teams) may be shifted toward topics or stories that are perceived to perform well on social platforms, while low-engagement topics may receive reduced resources or only wire coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Algorithmic feedback can influence newsroom investment decisions; be aware of possible bias against less 'clickable' but important stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Influence on content presentation and framing
rubrics_metrics.description: Algorithms influence how stories are framed and presented (headline tweaks, choice of photo/video, angle) to 'get Facebook’s algorithm to cooperate,' while journalists try to keep framing aligned with editorial standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Modify presentation where it aligns with editorial judgement; avoid manufacturing framing solely for algorithmic advantage if it conflicts with journalistic ethics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations due to algorithmic opacity
rubrics_metrics.description: Opaque, proprietary nature of algorithms limits journalists' ability to know why content performs well or poorly, which constrains the weight given to algorithmic explanations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat algorithmic inferences as tentative 'folk theories'; be cautious about attributing causality to algorithmic reasons without corroborating evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organizational-level moderators
rubrics_metrics.description: A newsroom’s business model, size/brand, medium (broadcast, print, online), and editorial focus moderate how much algorithms influence editorial practice (e.g., for-profit ad-driven newsrooms are more attentive to algorithms).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess organizational incentives: larger national brands may deprioritize viral chasing; niche or commercial outlets may emphasize social distribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Routine-level moderators
rubrics_metrics.description: Day-to-day newsroom routines—how central social platforms are to workflow and whether social/audience engagement roles exist—influence how strongly algorithmic considerations shape decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presence of audience engagement editors often mediates and translates algorithmic expectations for reporters; training and routines determine uptake.

rubrics_metrics.name: Individual-level moderators
rubrics_metrics.description: Individual journalists’ roles, responsibilities, and normative commitments shape the degree to which their 'folk theories' affect editorial choices; social-media-specific roles are more likely to apply algorithmic thinking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize role-based differences in influence; senior editors and specialized social editors may have disproportionate sway over practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Algorithmic 'folk theories' as guiding heuristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists form informal, non-authoritative 'folk theories' about how algorithms work, drawn from platform communication, experimentation, press, and peer discussions, which guide their behavior despite possible inaccuracies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat these heuristics as socially produced sense-making tools; validate with analytics where possible and avoid over-reliance on untested assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Algorithmic incentives toward sensational or outrage-inducing content
rubrics_metrics.description: Participants perceived algorithms as privileging content that provokes strong reactions (outrage, gruesome imagery) because such content drives engagement and keeps users on platforms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be mindful of ethical costs of optimizing for outrage; guard against sensationalism that undermines public-interest journalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of analytics and web metrics in gatekeeping
rubrics_metrics.description: Web analytics and audience metrics serve as feedback that influence newsroom gatekeeping and may re-shape priorities (e.g., moving resources toward locally engaging stories after low engagement on national topics).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporate analytics to inform but not dictate editorial judgment; triangulate metrics with editorial values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Isomorphism through algorithms / institutional dependency
rubrics_metrics.description: Platforms' algorithmic logics can produce institutional isomorphism—news organizations aligning practices to what platforms deem relevant—thus reshaping conceptions of newsworthiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monitor for systemic shifts in editorial norms driven by platform incentives; preserve newsroom autonomy where public interest requires divergence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negotiated journalistic autonomy
rubrics_metrics.description: The extent to which algorithmic considerations influence editorial choices is negotiated: algorithms introduce new impulses but do not fully displace journalists' normative autonomy to decide what is newsworthy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain explicit discussions and policies about when to prioritize editorial principles over distribution optimization; document rationale for decisions influenced by algorithmic considerations.
